name: False positive paradox
title: False Positive Paradox Calculator
desc: Discover why "accurate" tests can be misleading with this false positive paradox calculator.

m.l: Select a scenario or create your own

c: Suppose a disease affects 1% of the population, and that's the only information you know about your risk of getting ill. A new medical test is 98% accurate in detecting the disease. In other words, if you're healthy, there's a 98% chance the test will detect it; similarly, if you're ill, it's also 98% probably the test will diagnose it. You take the test and receive a positive result. What is the

Suppose that out of 100,000 passengers, only one is a terrorist. A new scanning system detects with 99.9% accuracy if a terrorist is a terrorist and with 98% accuracy if a non-terrorist is a non-terrorist. If the machine scans you and indicates that you are a terrorist, what is the probability that you are actually a terrorist?
Wrong. Do you want to try again? Then select another answer.
Tip: The correct answer is higher.
Tip: The correct answer is lower.

m.h: Probability of a true negative being correctly identified.
Probability of a true positive being correctly identified.
Positive predictive value.

c: For example, if we apply the test to 100,000 randomly selected people, we'll have two groups and four sub-groups: Positives (P): There will be 1000 of them, as the chance of having the disease is 1% (1000 out of 100,000). True positives (TP): The probability of testing positive if you're within that 1% of positive people: 980 out of 1000 (98%). False negative (FN): The probability of testing negat

Let's say the machine scans 100 million passengers: Positives (P): Only 1000 out of those 100 million would be actual terrorists. True positives (TP): Of the 1000 terrorist passengers, the system will correctly identify 99.9% of them as positive, meaning there will be 999 true positives. False negatives (FN): 1% of those terrorists will not be identified by the system, meaning there'll be 1 false
This is the probability tree that will be filled in when number of tested elements is provided:

Therefore, if you receive a positive test result, the probability that you actually have the disease is: TP/(TP + FP) = {{true_positives.formattedValue}}/({{true_positives.formattedValue}} + {{false_positives.formattedValue}}) ≈ 33%

Therefore, if the machine indicates you're a terrorist, the probability that you're actually one is: TP/(TP + FP) = {{true_positives.formattedValue}}/({{true_positives.formattedValue}} + {{false_positives.formattedValue}}) ≈ 0.05%
You can also look at the following confusion matrix, where PP stands for predictive positives and PN for predicted negatives:

Such probability is known as the positive predictive value (PPV), and it doesn't depend on the number of people examined but on the prevalence of the condition, specificity, and (slightly) sensitivity.

m.l: Calculate MOE with Finite Population Correction (FPC)?
m.h: The FPC factor is used when the sample is 5 or more percent of the entire population.

c: Are you sure the sample size and the population size are the same?
The general rule says the FPC factor should be included when the sample is at least 5% of the population.

When the sample size equals the population size, you are sampling the entire population, meaning there is no sampling error—you have the exact population parameters. In this case, the concept of a margin of error does not apply because you are not estimating from a sample; you have the full population data.

name: Monty Hall problem
title: Monty Hall Problem Calculator
desc: The Monty Hall Problem calculator can help you win a car 66% of the time — but only if you play the game!

m.l: Do you want to play or simulate?

c: Out of {{number_sim.formattedValue}} games, the player that always changes door won the car {{carcount.formattedValue}} times.  As a bonus, here's {{goatcount.formattedValue}} goats.
Out of {{number_sim.formattedValue}} games, the player that always keeps the door won the car {{carcount.formattedValue}} times.  This means {{goatcount.formattedValue}} goats.
That's a hefty tribe of goats!
You have three closed doors in front of you. Two of them hide a goat, the third hides a car. Choose a door, then follow the instructions, and try to end up opening the door with the car!
We'll open door number {{openn.value}} for you. There's a goat there!  Do you want to change door, or to keep your choice?
You choose to change your door! Your final choice is to open the door {{change.value}}! Are you ready to see if you won or not?
You choose not to change your door. Your final choice is to open the door {{choice_door.value}}! Are you ready to see if you won or not?
The door revealed a car! You won the game!
We're afraid that's a goat. However, goats are very friendly and smart animals: we don't consider it a loss!
Play again to try your luck: press the reload button, or read the article to learn the math behind this intriguing paradox!

c: We use the Z-score if the test statistic approximately follows the standard normal distribution. You can count on the approximation if you have a large sample (say at least 50 data points) and treat your distribution as normal.

Use the t-score option if your test statistic follows the t-Student distribution. This distribution has a shape similar to a normal distribution (bell-shaped and symmetric) but has heavier tails – the exact shape depends on the parameter called the degrees of freedom.

This distribution arises if, for example, you take the sum of squared variables, each following the normal distribution. You can also check the goodness of fit or independence between two variables with the χ² test.

c: Parrondo's paradox describes the counterintuitive result of how two losing games can produce a winning game. Picture the following scenario: You have two games (game A and game B) in which you flip a loaded coin whose odds are specific to the game. Every time you win a game, you earn $1 — otherwise, you lose $1. Game A: In this game, you have a 0.495 chance to win. Game B: Here, your odds depend o

opts: A, A, B, B, A, A, ...

c: Below, you will find a simulation of thousands of 100-game runs starting at $0. You can select the strategy by which you'd choose which games are played: — Play only Game A; — Play only Game B; — Play one game of A followed by one game of B and repeat; — Play two games of A followed by two games of B and repeat; or — Randomly pick between both games.
After simulating {{totalRuns.formattedValue}} runs of {{numberOfGames.formattedValue}} games each, the average end capital is ${{averageEndCap.formattedValue}}.
As you see, even if you play two losing games, you can mix them up to produce a winning game! How is this possible? Check the text paired with this calculator to learn more.
